'''ahuatle''' (ä-ö-ät′l), ''n.'' [Mex.] A preparation of the eggs of a dipterous insect of Mexico, ''Ephydra hians'', used for food.

{{smaller block|It is of the eggs of this insect . . . that the greater part of the food products of this lake [Lake Texcoco], known as ''Ahuatle'', is composed. . . . The eggs are . . . cleaned and ground into flour, which is called ''Ahuatle''. This food is deemed suitable for those days in which the religious observances prohibit the use of flesh. It is prepared by mixing with hens’ eggs and fried with fat in small cakes. The taste is similar to that of caviare.
{{right|''Stand. Nat. Hist.'', II. 432.}}}}

'''a-huff†''' (ạ-huf′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''huff.''] In a swaggering manner.

{{smaller block|Set cap ''a-huff'', and challenge him the field.
{{right|''Greene'', James IV., iv.}}}}

'''ahull†''' (ạ-hul′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup>, on, in, + ''hull.''] ''Naut.'', in or into the position of a ship when her sails are furled and the helm is lashed to the lee side; in the position of a vessel when she lies to, with all her sails furled.

'''ahungered†''' (ạ-hung′gėrd), ''a.'' or ''pp.'' [Also ''anhungered'', < ME. ''ahungred'', ''ahungryd'', ''anhungred'',
readings.c1s2:

''of-hyngred'', pp. of ''of-hyngrian'', cause to hunger, < ''of-'' intensive + ''hyngrian'', cause to hunger: see ''a-''<sup>4</sup> and ''hunger'', ''v.'' Cf. ''athirst.''] Pinched with hunger; hungry. [Erroneously printed in the New Testament as two words, in the forms (in different editions) ''a hungered'', ''an hungered'', and ''an hungred.'']

'''ahungry†''' (ạ-hung′gri), ''a.'' [Same as ''ahungered'', with suffix changed in imitation of ''hungry.''] Hungry: as, “I am not ''a-hungry,''” ''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 1.

'''Ahuramazda''' (ä″hö-ra-maz′dä̤), ''n.'' [Zend ''Ahuro mazdao'', > Pers. ''Ormuzd.''] Same as ''Ormuzd''.

'''ahyu''' (ä′ū), ''n.'' [Jap.] The ai, a Japanese salmonoid fish, ''Salmo'' (''Plecoglossus'') ''altivelis'', also known as the one-year fish. It is catadromous, and an annual.
{{smaller block|The ''ahyu'' is specially worthy of record as the only fish known to combine the habits of the two classes [of catadromous and annual fishes].
{{right|''Gill'', Smithsonian Rep., 1883, p. 726.}}}}

'''ai<sup>1</sup>.''' [(1) < ME. ''ai'', ''ay'', ''ei'', ''ey'', ''æi'', ''aȝ'', ''eȝ'', ''æȝ'', < AS. ''æg'', ''eg'', ''ǣg'', ''ēg'', that is, the vowel ''æ'' or ''e'', ''ǣ'' or ''ē'', followed by the palatal ''g'', in ME. ''g'', ''ȝ'', or ''y'', also written ''i'', merging with vowel ''y'' or ''i'': see ''g'', ''y'', ''i''. (The digraph in ''hair'', ME. ''here'', has taken the
readings.c1s3:
place of earlier ''e'' as in ''ere'', ''there'', ''their'', etc.) (2) < ME. ''ai'', ''ay'', ''ei'', ''ey'', with following vowel ''aie'', etc., < OF. ''ai'', ''ei'', etc., of various origin, usually developed from L. ''a'' or ''e''. (3) Of various other origin. See examples cited below.] A common English digraph, representing generally the sound of “long ''a''” (ā), which becomes ã before ''r'', as in ''ail'' (sounded like ''ale''), ''vain'' (sounded like ''vane'', ''vein''), ''air'' (sounded like ''ere'', ''heir''), etc. {{smaller|As commonly pronounced, it is strictly a diphthong consisting of “long ''a''” (ā), or ''e'' (e), followed by a vanish, ''i'' (i), which is, in words of Anglo-Saxon origin, historically identical with the consonant ''y''. This digraph occurs in words—(1) of Anglo-Saxon origin, as in ''ail'', ''hail''<sup>1</sup>, ''nail'', ''sail'', ''fain'', ''wain'', ''fair''<sup>1</sup>, ''lair'', etc., being also used, parallel with ''ae'', in modern Scotch spelling for “long ''a''” equivalent to E. “long ''o'',” ''oa'', ''o-e'', as in ''aith'', ''raid'', ''ain'', etc., =E. ''oath'', ''road'', ''rode'', ''own'', etc.; (2) of French, and ultimate Latin origin, as in ''fail'', ''faint'', ''vain'', ''grain'', ''aim'', ''fair''<sup>2</sup>, etc.; (3) of Greek origin, being used sometimes as a direct transliteration of Greek αι instead of the usual Latin transliteration ''ae'' or ''æ'' (see ''æ''<sup>1</sup>), as in ''aitiology'', etc.; (4) of various other origin, usually representing the diphthong äi or ī, as in German ''kaiser'' and Oriental and “native” words, especially proper names, as ''Aino'', ''Cairo'', etc. In the words of Anglo-Saxon and French origin ''ai'' varied with ''ay'', which now prevails when final, usually changing back to ''ai'' when made medial by the addition of a suffix, as in ''day'', ''clay'', ''gay'', ''affray'', ''array'', etc., ''daily'', ''afraid'', ''raiment'', etc.; but in some such cases, especially before a suffix beginning with a vowel, ''ay'' remains unchanged, as in ''payment'', ''betrayed'', ''clayey'', etc.}}

'''ai<sup>2</sup>''' (ä′ē), ''n.'' [=F. ''aï'', ''hay'', < Braz. ''aï'', ''haï'' (Mahn).] The three-toed sloth, ''Bradypus tridactylus'' or ''torquatus'': so called from having a feeble, plaintive cry somewhat resembling the sound represented by its name. See ''sloth'' and ''Bra-''

'''aidant''' (ā′dant), ''a.'' [< OF. ''aidant'', ppr. of ''aider'', < L. ''adjutan(t-)s'', ppr. of ''adjutare'', aid: see ''aid''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', and ''adjutant.''] Helping; helpful; supplying aid. [Rare.]

{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 4.}}}}

'''aid-de-camp,''' ''n.'' See ''aide-de-camp.''

'''aide''' (ād), ''n.'' Same as ''aide-de-camp.''
{{smaller block|[Hamilton] was picked out by Washington to serve as his confidential ''aide.''
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXIII. 117.}}}}

'''aide-de-camp''' (E. pron. ād′dẹ̄-kamp, F. pron. ād′dė-koṅ), ''n.''; pl. ''aides-de-camp'' (ādz′dẹ̄-kamp or ādz′dė-koṅ). [< F. ''aide de camp'', lit. a field assistant: ''aide'', aid, assistant (see ''aid''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''); ''de'', < L. ''de'', of; ''camp'', < L. ''campus'', field, battlefield: see ''camp''<sup>1</sup>.] ''Milit.'', a confidential officer whose duty it is to receive and communicate the orders
readings.c3s2:
of a general officer, act as his secretary upon occasion, and the like. Sometimes written ''aid-de-camp.''

'''aider''' (ā′dėr), ''n.'' One who helps; an assistant or auxiliary; an abetter; an accessory.
{{smaller block|All along as he went were punished the adherents and ''aiders'' of the late rebels.
{{right|''Burnet.''}}}}
{{smaller block|[Emerson] was the friend and ''aider'' of those who would live in the spirit.
{{right|''M. Arnold.''}}}}

'''aides-de-camp,''' ''n.'' Plural of ''aide-de-camp.''

'''aidful''' (ād′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''aid''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful.''] Giving aid; helpful. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Aidful'' to the distresses of God’s people.
{{right|''Bp. Hall,'' Haman Disrespected.}}}}

'''aidless''' (ād′les), ''a.'' [< ''aid''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.''] Without aid; helpless; without succor; unsupported.

'''aid-major†''' (ād′mā″jọr), ''n.'' Same as ''adjutant.''

'''aid-prayer''' (ād′prãr), ''n.'' A petition or plea formerly employed in actions concerning estates in land, by which a defendant claimed the assistance of another person jointly interested with him in sustaining the title.

'''aiglet'''<sup>1</sup> (ā′glet), ''n.'' [Dim. of OF. ''aigle,'' eagle: see ''eaglet.''] In ''her.'', an eaglet or young eagle.

'''aiglet'''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' See ''aglet.''

'''aigocerine,''' ''a.'' See ''ægocerine.''

'''Aigocerus,''' ''n.'' See ''Ægocerus.''

'''aigre'''<sup>1</sup>'''†''' (ā′gėr), ''a.'' [< F. ''aigre:'' see ''eager''<sup>1</sup>.] Sharp; sour. See ''eager''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|Like ''aigre'' droppings into milk.
{{right|''Shak.'' (1623), Hamlet, i. 5.}}}}

'''aigremore''' (ā′gėr-mōr), ''n.'' [F.; origin unknown.] Charcoal made ready for the admixture of the other constituent materials of gunpowder.

In ''bot.'', same as ''egret''.—'''4.''' In ''ichth.'', a labroid fish, ''Lachnolæmus maximus'', better known as the ''hogfish'' (which see).

'''aigue-marine''' (āg-mạ-rēn′), ''n.'' [F.] Same as ''aquamarine''.

'''aid'''<sup>1</sup> (ād), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''aiden'', < OF. ''aider'', also ''eider'', ''aidier'', mod. F. ''aider'' = Pr. ''ajudar'', < L. ''adjutare'', help, aid, freq. of ''adjuvare'', pp. ''adjutus'', help, < ''ad'', to, + ''juvare'', help: see ''adjutant'', ''adjute''.]   '''1.''' To help; assist; afford support or relief; promote the desire, purpose, or action of: as, to ''aid'' a person in his business, or an animal in its efforts; to ''aid'' a medicine in its operation.
{{smaller block|<poem>Till more hands
''Aid'' us, the work under our labour grows,
Luxurious by restraint.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ix. 208.}}}}
{{smaller block|So ''aid'' me Heaven when at mine uttermost.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}
'''2.''' To promote the course or accomplishment of; help in advancing or bringing about; forward; facilitate: as, to ''aid'' the recovery of a patient, or the operation of a machine; to ''aid'' one’s designs.
{{smaller block|<poem>Take your choice of those
That best can ''aid'' your action.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cor., i. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|No more these scenes my meditation ''aid''.
{{right|''Pope'', Eloisa to Abelard, l. 161.}}}}
{{smaller block|[In this sense ''aid'' is often followed by ''in'', giving it the appearance of an intransitive verb, the direct object of assistance being unexpressed: as, he actively ''aided in'' the search.]—'''Aiding and abetting''', in ''criminal law'', an offense committed by one who, though not directly perpetrating a crime, is yet present at its commission and renders aid to the perpetrator. ='''Syn.''' To support, sustain, serve, back, second, abet, coöperate with, relieve.}}

'''aid'''<sup>1</sup> (ād), ''n.''   [< F. ''aide'', < OF. ''aide'', ''eide'', etc.; from the verb.]   '''1.''' Help; succor; support; assistance.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sweet father, I behold him in my dreams
Gaunt as it were the skeleton of himself,</poem> Death-pale, for lack of gentle maiden’s ''aid.''
{{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}

'''2.''' He who or that which aids or yields assistance; a helper; an auxiliary; an assistant: as, Coleridge’s “''Aids'' to Reflection.”

{{smaller block|It is not good that man should be alone; let us make unto him an ''aid'' like unto himself.{{right|Tobit viii. 6.}}}}

{{smaller block|The ''aids'' to noble life are all within.
{{right|''M. Arnold'', Worldly Place.}}}}

'''3.''' In ''feudal law'', a customary payment made by a tenant or vassal to his lord, originally a voluntary gift; hence, in ''Eng. hist.'', applied to the forms of taxation employed by the crown between the Norman conquest and the fourteenth century. {{smaller|Aids in the narrower sense, whether to the crown or mesne lords, were by Magna Charta limited to grants on three special occasions: (''a'') to ransom the lord when a prisoner; (''b'') to make the lord’s eldest son a knight; (''c'') the marriage of the lord’s eldest daughter. The legal authority to enforce such aids was abolished in 1660.}}

{{smaller block|First there were payments called ''aids;'' in the theory of our earlier authors they were offered of the tenant’s free will, to meet the costs incurred by the lord on particular occasions; but they settled into a fixed custom afterwards, if they had not really done so when those authors wrote.
{{right|''F. Pollock'', Land Laws, iii.}}}}

{{smaller block|The marriage was, according to the new feudal ideas, made the excuse for a heavy exaction of money, an ''aid'', as the feudal lawyers call it.
{{right|''E. A. {{smaller block|[Hamilton] was picked out by Washington to serve as his confidential ''aide.''
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXXIII. 117.}}}}

'''aide-de-camp''' (E. pron. ād′dẹ̄-kamp, F. pron. ād′dė-koṅ), ''n.''; pl. ''aides-de-camp'' (ādz′dẹ̄-kamp or ādz′dė-koṅ).   [< F. ''aide de camp'', lit. a field assistant: ''aide'', aid, assistant (see ''aid''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''); ''de'', < L. ''de'', of; ''camp'', < L. ''campus'', field, battlefield: see ''camp''<sup>1</sup>.]   ''Milit.'', a confidential officer whose duty it is to receive and communicate the orders of a general officer, act as his secretary upon occasion, and the like. Sometimes written ''aid-de-camp.''

'''aider''' (ā′dėr), ''n.'' One who helps; an assistant or auxiliary; an abetter; an accessory.
{{smaller block|All along as he went were punished the adherents and ''aiders'' of the late rebels.
{{right|''Burnet.''}}}}
{{smaller block|[Emerson] was the friend and ''aider'' of those who would live in the spirit.
{{right|''M. Arnold.''}}}}

'''aides-de-camp,''' ''n.'' Plural of ''aide-de-camp.''

'''aidful''' (ād′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''aid''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful.'']   Giving aid; helpful. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|''Aidful'' to the distresses of God’s people.
{{right|''Bp. Hall,'' Haman Disrespected.}}}}

'''aidless''' (ād′les), ''a.''   [< ''aid''<sup>1</sup> + ''-less.'']   Without aid; helpless; without succor; unsupported.

'''aid-major†''' (ād′mā″jọr), ''n.'' Same as ''adjutant.''

'''aid-prayer''' (ād′prãr), ''n.'' A petition or plea formerly employed in actions concerning estates in land, by which a defendant claimed the assistance of another person jointly interested with him in sustaining the title.

'''aiglet'''<sup>1</sup> (ā′glet), ''n.''   [Dim. of OF. ''aigle,'' eagle: see ''eaglet.'']   In ''her.'', an eaglet or young eagle.

'''aiglet'''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'' See ''aglet.''

'''aigocerine,''' ''a.'' See ''ægocerine.''

'''Aigocerus,''' ''n.'' See ''Ægocerus.''

'''aigre'''<sup>1</sup>'''†''' (ā′gėr), ''a.''   [< F. ''aigre:'' see ''eager''<sup>1</sup>.]   Sharp; sour. See ''eager''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|Like ''aigre'' droppings into milk.
{{right|''Shak.'' (1623), Hamlet, i. 5.}}}}

'''aigre<sup>2</sup>''' (ā′gėr), ''n.'' See ''eager''<sup>2</sup>.

'''aigremore''' (ā′gėr-mōr), ''n.''   [F.; origin unknown.]   Charcoal made ready for the admixture of the other constituent materials of gunpowder.

'''aigret, aigrette''' (ā′gret, ā-gret′), ''n.''   [< F. ''aigrette'': see ''egret''.]   '''1.''' The small white heron. {{img float|file=century v01 p0146 c3f1.png|width=148px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Aigret. {{smaller|(From Hans Burgkmair’s “Triumph of Maximilian I.”)}}}}}} See ''egret''.—'''2.''' (''a'') A plume composed of feathers arranged in imitation of the feathers on the head of the heron, and worn on helmets or by ladies as a part of their head-dress, etc. (''b'') A copy in jewelry of such a plume, often so made that the seeming feathers tremble with the movements of the wearer, causing the gems to sparkle.—'''3.''' In ''bot.'', same as ''egret''.—'''4.''' In ''ichth.'', a labroid fish, ''Lachnolæmus maximus'', better known as the ''hogfish'' (which see).

'''aigue-marine''' (āg-mạ-rēn′), ''n.''   [F.]   Same as ''aquamarine''.
